title: EFFECTS OF COLOR TEMPERATURE ON PROJECTED FRACTAL LIGHT PATTERNS: VISUAL INTEREST AND EMOTIONAL RESPONSE
research_question: The study aimed to examine the effects of color temperature of projected fractal patterns on visual interest and emotional response in interior spaces. Specifically, Phase 1 investigated which two-dimensional fractal pattern complexity is most visually interesting and its influence on emotional response. Phase 2 investigated whether different color temperatures of natural light influence the choice of three-dimensional fractal pattern complexity and its effect on emotional response.

participants.description: Sixty undergraduate and graduate students enrolled in İhsan Doğramacı Bilkent University. Phase 1: 30 participants (20 female, 10 male, 93.3% aged 18-27). Phase 2: 30 different participants (23 female, 7 male, 76.7% aged 18-27). Participants with prior knowledge on color or lighting, or uncorrectable eye deficiencies were excluded.
participants.recruitment: Participants were selected by random sampling method. Participation was entirely voluntary and no reward was provided.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Five different complexity levels of two-dimensional statistical fractal patterns (D = 1.1, D = 1.3, D = 1.5, D = 1.7, D = 1.9) displayed on a computer screen.

Three-dimensional projected fractal patterns (D = 1.1, D = 1.3, D = 1.5, D = 1.7, D = 1.9) with three different natural light color temperatures (4000K - noon sky, 6500K - overcast sky, 12000K - clear sky) in a simulated interior space (6.2x5m, 3m ceiling, achromatic colors, smooth walls).

measures.instrument: Two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) paired comparison test
Mehrabian and Russell (M-R) model adapted from Bradley and Lang’s (1994) PAD model, 6 bipolar adjective pairs (e.g., unhappy-happy) on a 5-point semantic differential scale.
Mehrabian and Russell (M-R) model adapted from Bradley and Lang’s (1994) PAD model, 6 bipolar adjective pairs (e.g., relaxed-stimulated) on a 5-point semantic differential scale.

mechanisms: Fractal fluency theory: human visual system's adaptation to mid-complexity fractal patterns found in nature.
Curvilinear relationship between visual complexity, visual interest, and preference (Berlyne, 1970).
implementation_implications: Designers can implement natural light patterns to create visually interesting interior spaces.
Findings guide interior architects and façade designers in implementing fractal patterns for creating more visually interesting interior spaces.

limitations: Spatial variables of projection (projection surfaces, view direction, material properties, and pattern size) were kept under control, limiting generalizability to other configurations.
Behavioral intentions of participants were not examined due to time restriction.
The scale of projected fractal patterns in proportion to the space was not varied.
Demographic variables (age, gender, culture, educational background) were not examined for their influence on visual interest and emotional response.
